(i) a process-based model coupled to a radiative transfer model can simulate the MODIS vegetation index with good accuracy and (ii) the inverse modeling approach is a useful tool to improve model parameterization.

1) we developed a new version of BIOME BGC (PROSAILH BGC), 2) we developed a two-step inversion approach, and 3) we applied the model and the inversion approach to the case study of poplar plantation in Northern Italy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and validation of a process-based model to estimate GPP in agro-forestry ecosystems.
the development of a new version of the BIOME-BG model (named PROSIL-BGC) which allows the simulation of the radiative regime within the canopy.

the development of a new version of the BIOME-BCG model coupled with the PROSAIL radiative transfer model, and with the development of an inverse modeling approach to optimize model parameters, phenology and biomass.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the inverse modeling approach was able to provide a good description of the carbon budget at a regional scale, but that further improvements are needed in the description of the radiation regime within the canopy.
the assimilation of satellite-derived information in a process-based model may be a powerful tool for the estimation of gross primary production at large scale.
the PROSILH-BGC coupled with an inverse modeling approach was shown to be a promising tool for modeling gross primary productivity of poplar plantatios in Northern Italy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a process-based model, such as BIOME-BGC, can be successfully applied to simulate the gross primary production of agro-forestry plantations at regional scale by using information derived from satellite and flux data.
the use of a process model coupled with an inverse modeling approach may be a powerful tool to estimate the gross carbon budget of agro-forestry ecosystems.
the use of remote sensing data, in combination with eddy covariance flux data, may be a promising tool to improve the accuracy of GPP predictions in agroforestry ecosystems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can now use the inverse modeling approach to estimate gross primary production in poplar plantations and in other ecosystems.
the PROSILH-BGC model can be used to estimate gross primary production at the regional scale with good accuracy, provided that a suitable inverse modeling approach is used.
the inverse modeling approach may be a useful tool for optimizing ecophysiological model paramaters, phenological dates, and parameters related to standing biomass.
